hubs.name: Wellbeing & Health
hubs.tagline: Emotional resilience, rest, and whole-person care.
hubs.intro: This hub gathers books on how people actually feel better: working with difficult emotions, sleeping and recovering from stress, and understanding the older healing systems that treat body and mind together. Contemplative and clinical voices sit side by side here, and each listing says which one it is.

hubs.name: Meditation, Yoga & Mantra
hubs.tagline: Practice-first books: sit, breathe, move, chant.
hubs.intro: The practice shelf. Start with secular mindfulness, move into the postural and philosophical sides of yoga, or learn how Sanskrit sound is used in devotional and meditative practice. Where a method belongs to a particular lineage, the book page names it.

hubs.name: Religions & Sacred Texts
hubs.tagline: Primary scriptures, serious translations, and clear guides.
hubs.intro: Scripture and the scholarship around it, organised by tradition rather than blended together. Hinduism, Buddhism, Taoism, Gnostic and Christian mystical literature are kept distinct, with a comparative-religion department for readers who want to see how they differ.

hubs.name: Occult, Magick & Paganism
hubs.tagline: Western esoteric currents, from Hermetic texts to modern Wicca.
hubs.intro: Hermeticism, alchemy, witchcraft, Wicca, paganism, tarot and astrology each have their own history and vocabulary. We separate historical sources, modern religious movements and divinatory practice, so readers know what kind of book they are opening.

hubs.name: Energy & Inner Cultivation
hubs.tagline: Qigong, neigong, subtle-body maps and internal training.
hubs.intro: Books on cultivating inner energy, mainly Chinese qigong and neigong traditions and the Indian subtle-body models of chakras and kundalini. These are different systems with different vocabularies. Practice claims are reported as the authors present them.

hubs.name: Consciousness, Myth & Ancient Wisdom
hubs.tagline: Mind, dreams, myth, and the oldest surviving texts.
hubs.intro: Philosophy of awareness, dream work, comparative mythology and ancient literature. Readers can move between a non-dual teacher, a psychologist of religion and a translation of a Mesopotamian epic, and still know which voice they are hearing.

hubs.name: Fantasy, Folklore & Supernatural Fiction
hubs.tagline: Wizards, myths retold, fairy tales and the uncanny.
hubs.intro: Storytelling shelves for readers who follow magic into fiction. Modern fantasy, classic gothic and supernatural novels, collected folk and fairy tales, and philosophy that sits beside them are kept distinct from the religious and practice books elsewhere in the store, so a novel is never mistaken for a manual.

departments.name: Emotional Wellbeing
departments.intro: Books on grief, anxiety, trauma, self-compassion and the stress-illness connection. Some are clinical and some contemplative; the book pages say which, and none replaces professional care.

departments.name: Sleep & Stress
departments.intro: Evidence-led guides to rest, recovery and the physiology of stress, plus contemplative approaches to calming the nervous system.

departments.name: Holistic Traditions
departments.intro: Traditional systems that treat body, mind and environment as one whole, such as Ayurveda, Chinese medicine and herbal lore. Entries describe what each tradition claims and are not medical advice.

departments.name: Mindfulness
departments.intro: Attention training from secular stress-reduction courses to the Buddhist teachings they grew from. Look for the tradition label to see whether a book is clinical, devotional or both.

departments.name: Yoga
departments.intro: Postural yoga, the classical Yoga Sutras, and the wider philosophy behind them. Modern posture manuals and classical texts are separated so readers can choose by purpose.

departments.name: Sanskrit & Mantras
departments.intro: Guides to the sound, meaning and traditional use of Sanskrit mantras, including the Gayatri, Maha Mrityunjaya and Shakti mantras. Look for notes on pronunciation, lineage and whether initiation is traditionally expected.

departments.name: Hinduism
departments.intro: The Vedic, Upanishadic, epic and devotional literature of Hindu traditions, with accessible translations alongside scholarly introductions.

departments.name: Tantra
departments.intro: Tantra is a family of Hindu and Buddhist ritual and contemplative traditions. It is often confused with modern Western 'neo-tantra', so each book is labelled with the approach it takes.

departments.name: Buddhism
departments.intro: Theravada, Zen, Tibetan and other Buddhist schools, from foundational teachings to modern commentary. Schools are named so that different lineages are not blended.

departments.name: Taoism
departments.intro: Philosophical Taoism (Laozi, Zhuangzi), religious Taoism and internal alchemy. The Tao Te Ching and later cultivation manuals are different kinds of literature, and we shelve them accordingly.

departments.name: Qigong
departments.intro: Chinese energy-cultivation practices combining movement, breath and attention. Books vary from health-oriented routines to martial and spiritual lineages.

departments.name: Neigong
departments.intro: Neigong (nei kung) means 'internal work': training the body's inner structure and energy, often in martial or Taoist-influenced contexts. It overlaps with qigong but is not identical to it.

departments.name: Mo Pai
departments.intro: Mo Pai is a neigong lineage presented to English readers mainly through the Mo Pai Nei Kung books. Its lineage history comes from the authors' own accounts and has not been independently documented by academic sources.

departments.name: Comparative Religion
departments.intro: Surveys and cross-tradition studies that explain how faiths differ as well as where they converge. A good place to begin if you have not chosen one tradition yet.

departments.name: Gnosticism
departments.intro: The Nag Hammadi library and related early Christian-era texts that teach salvation through knowledge (gnosis). Gnosticism is distinct from Hermeticism, though both are often shelved together.

departments.name: Christian Mysticism
departments.intro: Contemplative writings from the Desert Fathers through medieval and Carmelite mystics. These are orthodox-tradition works and are not Gnostic.

departments.name: Hermeticism
departments.intro: The Hermetica (late-antique Greek and Egyptian-influenced texts) and the traditions built on them. Modern books such as the Kybalion are part of the later reception, not the ancient corpus.

departments.name: Alchemy
departments.intro: Practical, spiritual and psychological alchemy. Historical treatises, Taoist internal alchemy and Jungian readings are shelved separately because they answer different questions.

departments.name: Witchcraft
departments.intro: Historical witchcraft, folk magic and modern witchcraft practice. Historical studies and how-to guides are labelled so you know which you are reading.

departments.name: Spells & Folk Magic
departments.intro: Spell collections, charms and reference works on magical practice. Entries describe what the author teaches; the catalogue makes no claims about efficacy.

departments.name: Wicca
departments.intro: Wicca is a modern initiatory and eclectic religion founded in the twentieth century. It is a specific religion within the broader pagan family, not a synonym for witchcraft or paganism.

departments.name: Paganism
departments.intro: Contemporary and reconstructionist pagan religions, including Druidry, Heathenry and goddess spirituality, as distinct from Wicca and from the ancient religions they draw on.

departments.name: Tarot
departments.intro: Tarot as symbolic language for reflection and divination. Beginner guides, deep card-by-card studies and history are kept apart.

departments.name: Astrology
departments.intro: Natal, psychological and traditional astrology. The catalogue reports each author's method and makes no scientific claims for astrology.

departments.name: Subtle-Body Traditions
departments.intro: Chakras, nadis, kundalini and related maps of subtle anatomy. These come from Indian yoga and tantra and are often retold in modern Western frameworks; we flag which is which.

departments.name: Dreams
departments.intro: Dream interpretation, lucid dreaming and contemplative dream yoga, from Freud and Jung to Tibetan Buddhist practice.

departments.name: Consciousness
departments.intro: Non-dual teaching, psychology of religious experience and contemporary writing on awareness. Authors range from spiritual teachers to scientists.

departments.name: Ancient Texts
departments.intro: Primary sources in translation: epics, scriptures, funerary and wisdom literature. Where we know the translator, we name them, because translation choices matter.

departments.name: Mythology
departments.intro: Myth as story, symbol and comparative field. Classical, Norse, Mesopotamian, Indian and Mesoamerican traditions, with the scholars who interpret them.

departments.name: Fantasy
departments.intro: Epic, urban, historical and children's fantasy, from the schools of magic and quest tales many readers start with to long, layered series. Each entry is a novel; for the real traditions behind magic, see the occult and mythology shelves.

departments.name: Supernatural & Gothic Fiction
departments.intro: Ghost stories, vampires, haunted houses and gothic classics. Some are supernatural and some are scientific horror, and each book page says which.

departments.name: Folklore & Fairy Tales
departments.intro: Collected folk tales, fairy lore and the scholarship that studies them. Collections are labelled by how faithfully they follow their sources.

departments.name: Philosophy
departments.intro: Western philosophy and Stoic practice, from Plato to modern existential writing. These are works of argument and reflection, distinct from the scriptural and practice traditions elsewhere in the store.

traditions.name: Hindu / Vedic
traditions.intro: Traditions rooted in the Vedas, Upanishads, epics and devotional movements of the Indian subcontinent.

traditions.name: Tantric
traditions.intro: Ritual and contemplative systems found in both Hindu and Buddhist forms, distinct from modern Western neo-tantra.

traditions.name: Buddhist
traditions.intro: Theravada, Mahayana (including Zen) and Vajrayana traditions. Individual books name their school.

traditions.name: Taoist
traditions.intro: Philosophical and religious Taoism, including internal alchemy. Modern Healing Tao and related books are presented as contemporary adaptations.

traditions.name: Chinese Internal Arts
traditions.intro: Qigong, neigong and related training lineages. Often Taoist-influenced but a separate category from Taoist religion.

traditions.name: Gnostic
traditions.intro: Early Christian-era movements teaching salvation through direct knowledge, documented in the Nag Hammadi codices.

traditions.name: Christian
traditions.intro: Christian devotional and mystical literature, including contemplative writers of the medieval and Carmelite traditions.

traditions.name: Hermetic & Alchemical
traditions.intro: The Hermetica, medieval and Renaissance alchemy, and later Hermetic revivals.

traditions.name: Wiccan
traditions.intro: Wicca and its offshoots, a twentieth-century religious movement.

traditions.name: Pagan & Folk Magic
traditions.intro: Contemporary paganism, folk magic, and witchcraft beyond Wicca.

traditions.name: Western Esoteric
traditions.intro: Tarot, astrology, ceremonial magic and related Western occult currents.

traditions.name: Mythic & Ancient
traditions.intro: Texts and traditions of ancient civilisations: Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Scandinavia and the Americas.

traditions.name: Non-dual & Contemplative
traditions.intro: Teachers presenting awareness practice outside any single institutional religion, or in a non-sectarian form.

traditions.name: Secular / Clinical
traditions.intro: Psychology, medicine and science-led approaches to wellbeing.

traditions.name: Comparative
traditions.intro: Works that survey several traditions side by side.

traditions.name: Fiction: Fantasy & Supernatural
traditions.intro: Novels and story collections. These are works of imagination, not religious or instructional texts, even when they draw on myth or magical traditions.

traditions.name: Western Philosophy
traditions.intro: Philosophy in the Greek, Roman and European traditions, including Stoicism and existentialism.
